Here's what you have to understand about DSOTM.

For many people listening to it, it was the first thing of its kind.

In 1973, the prog rock scene consisted basically of this:

  1. Yes, who were pretty good but rather mainstream at this point

  2. Genesis, who were barely a thing by this time

  3. King Crimson, who hadn't had a hit album in years (Larks' Lounges in Aspic, which threw them back into the highlight, was released less than a month after DSOTM)

And that's it. Rush wouldn't become a thing for a year, and the psych movement that spawned prog was already long dead.

Further, at this point prog was still very far from the mainstream stations (except for Yes, the only prog album that was particularly popular at this point ITCOTCK, which released four years earlier), and prog music itself (the King Crimson/Genesis kind, that is) generally meant long-winded instrumentals, free form styling, and no real cohesion from song to song.

The mainstream rock music at this point consisted of bands such as Led Zeppelin and the emerging hard rock movement (Queen released their debut album shortly after DSOTM came out, to give some perspective). These bands, which received immense amounts of airplay, played short, radio-friendly songs that followed the typical style of pop music that the Beatles popularized a decade before.

 

And then, in March 1973, comes The Dark Side of the Moon. It's decisively progressive rock - it has the organs, the saxophones, the instrumentals, the few-and-far-between lyric styling, etc. But it was about as far away from mainstream pop rock as you could get. Its songs were long, but short enough to be played on the radio. Its lyrics provided something that no other genre really did at this time - words that you had to really think about to understand. Also, DSOTM wasn't just a record, it was a true album. One that commanded the listener drop the needle on "Breathe" and not move until "Eclipse" was done. That simply did not exist until DSOTM made it. Hell even Pink Floyd hadn't really done that before.

DSOTM, unlike any album before it, was like a musical painting - it had ten different layers for you to try and find and that's only on track one. Hell you could write a documentary about just the voice clips used on the album.

DSOTM represented not just PF's evolution in musicmaking, but also the change of the music industry as a whole away from The Beatles-style love songs and radio hits and towards a more meaningful sound. It was one of the first hugely successful albums to use an organ as a prime instrument (this had a huge effect in the popularization of the synthesizer later in the decade). In a way, it was the Elvis Presley of the 1970s - no piece of music recorded after DSOTM was quite the same as anything before it, and it influenced EVERYTHING after 1973.

There's a reason the album was on the billboard charts until they changed the rules and made it no longer eligible to be on it.

 

It wasn't the best PF album by far (I myself would rank The Wall and Animals above it), but it had such a massive effect on rock and music as a whole that it can't be downplayed at all.

You, in 2015, listen to this album and think "That was good", because you've had forty years of music that was influenced by it already under your belt. I don't think anybody in 2015 would listen to "Johnny B. Goode" and say "Wow, this is one of the ten greatest songs of all time!". Same thing with DSOTM - its legacy is what really makes it such a great album.

This is a bit of a cliche thing to say about DSotM, but it's true: it's more than just a collection of songs--it's a real album. A 40 minute-long experience. For example, take the Musique Concrète opener, Speak to Me. They didn't have to put that in the album. If it were just a collection of songs, then it could easily just start with the first song, Breathe, but they chose to have all those weird sound effects at the beginning. Why? To set the mood and to get you ready for the album, like a movie that opens with a few nice shots of scenery overlayed with credits rather than going straight into the first scene. Another example is the song On the Run. Going straight from Breathe to Time would have been fine, but a little boring, since the two songs are so similar (Time is really just another take on Breathe). However, putting On the Run, a weird synth-y interlude between those two songs creates a sense of pacing and tension. Stuff like this requires patience, sure, but it makes the payoff so much more satisfying.

The other big reason why this album is so important is the production. It isn't just four guys playing a bunch of songs with bass/drums/guitar/keys/vocals. They used the studio itself as an instrument. Weird sound effects here and there, heartbeats, clocks chiming, multiple overlaid keyboards with different effects, vaguely psychedelic guitar playing, all of this helps the album feel like a cohesive--maybe even cinematic--experience.

I also would like to know how you listened to this album. I definitely think the ideal DSotM experience is listening to it on a really good sound system. Nothing beats that. If you have a quality pair of headphones, that works too. On the other hand, if you listen to it with a pair of earbuds, or through crappy laptop/phone speakers, or even the built-in sound system of a car, you're not really listening to it properly.

Then again, it could just be that you don't love Dark Side of the Moon the way everyone else seems to. That's absolutely okay. There are plenty of bands that are considered "classic" and revolutionary but that I just don't really like all that much.

I also recommend that you listen to more Pink Floyd. Personally, I actually prefer Wish You Were Here and Animals. I also recommend checking out Meddle, and of course The Wall is a classic (though I personally think it's overrated).

I listened to it again through my in ear monitors (Shure SE-215) and it sounded much much better than my mac speakers. I have to say DSotM was really good, but I would appreciated it much more had I been around when it came out. But yeah, I see why people think it is great.

I don't even agree, but I was curious and googled a bit, and it means what it sounds like: the ability for states' governments to have legal standing (or 'rights') on par with or greater than federal legislation or mandate. Some examples given:

The right to determine what constitutes property under state law.

The right to be free of federal police power and the presence of federal soldiers within state territory.

The right to unilaterally secede from the Union.

The right to control export trade.

The right to be free from federal import taxes and tariffs.

The right to tax the transactions of the National Bank.

By extension, this is the reason that things like marriage equality and marijuana legalization are stuck waddling thru the federal system.

The right to determine what constitutes property under state law.

Slaves were considered property in the South, and this directly relates to that.

The right to be free of federal police power and the presence of federal soldiers within state territory.

The 3rd Amendment says "No Soldier shall, in time of peace be quartered in any house, without the consent of the Owner, nor in time of war, but in a manner to be prescribed by law." This supersedes state authority, as they agreed to.

The right to unilaterally secede from the Union.

Divorces are regulated by law. Secession would need to be agreed to and terms negotiated by both parties.

The right to control export trade.

Article 1, Section 8 (Powers of Congress) - "To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes;". This also supersedes state authority.

The right to be free from federal import taxes and tariffs.

Again, Article 1, Section 8 - "The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States; but all Duties, Imposts and Excises shall be uniform throughout the United States;". Again, superseded by national authority as they agreed to.

The right to tax the transactions of the National Bank.

Same part of Article 1, Section 8 quoted earlier. Powers of Taxation lie with Congress.
